To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
MART-1 and/or TYR mRNA is detected in peripheral blood from patients with metastatic malignant melanoma.

1) the presence of circulating melanoma cells in blood from patients with metastatic malignant melanoma can be detected with a quantitative RT-PCR assay, and 2) the presence of TYR but not MART-1 mRNA in blood is an independent predictor of poor survival.

MART-1 and/or TYR mRNA was detected in peripheral blood in 77% of patients with metastatic malignant melanoma and that the presence of TYR in the first or second blood sample was a trend towards an independent prognosticator for poor survival.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a quantitative RT-PCR assay for the detection of circulating melanoma cells and its application in patients with metastatic disease.

the detection of MART and TYR mRNA with a quantitative RT-PCR assay in blood samples from metastatic melanoma patients treated with cytokine therapy and the correlation between the results of the RT-PCR analysis and immunohistochemistry of the tumour cells.
the identification of melanoma cells by quantitative RT-PCR.

the presence of MART-1 or TYR mRNA in the peripheral blood is a poor prognostic indicator, but the clinical relevance of the assay needs to be further evaluated.
the quantitative RT-PCR assay used in this study can identify circulating melanoma cell in a proportion of patients with metastatic disease and may serve as a prognostic marker.
this study has shown that the presence of TYR or MART-1 mRNA in blood samples is not an independent prognostically significant marker in patients treated with immunotherapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the quantitative RT-PCR assay is a useful tool for the detection of circulating melanoma cells, but that the prognostic value of the assay needs further evaluation.

the detection of MART1 and TYR mRNAs in peripheral blood samples by quantitative RT-PCR is a feasible and sensitive method to monitor circulating melanoma cells, but that it does not appear to be a useful method to monitor response to immunotherapy in metastatic melanoma.
the presence of circulating melanoma cells in patients with metastatic disease is a common finding, but the clinical significance is not clear.
The main takeaway from our work is that
quantitative RT-PCR is a useful tool in the identification of circulating malignant cells in patients with melanoma.
the quantitative RT-PCR assay can be used to detect circulating melanoma cells in the blood.

quantitative RT-PCR can be used to detect MART-1 and/or TYR mRNA from circulating melanoma cells in the peripheral blood of melanoma patients and that the results correlate well with the presence of MART-1 protein and TYR protein expression in tumour cells.
